newsitem.title: UK: Merger means insurance dominated by two giants.
newsitem.headline: Merger means insurance dominated by two giants.

text.p: The international insurance sector has been reshaped by two major mergers in three months which have created two US superbrokers and left serious problems for their smaller British rivals.

Marsh & McLennan announced on Wednesday its plan to buy smaller U.S. rival Johnson & Higgins in a deal worth $1.8 billion. The two will combine their global insurance operations under the name J&H Marsh & McLennan Inc.

The move, the latest in wave of consolidation, means Marsh reclaims the position of world's largest broker which it held for 20 years before being overtaken by Aon in December with its acquisition of Alexander & Alexander.

In addition, it means the insurance industry is now dominated by two super-brokers. This time last year there were 'the big six'. Now, there are 'the big two' - Aon and Marsh, and the slightly smaller two - UK brokers Sedgwick and Willis Corroon.

The acquisition will be regarded as a bold comeback for Marsh, which had seen its insurance business lag, its share price undervalued, and its dominance undermined by the meteoric six-year rise of the aggressive Aon group achieved by buying up competitors on the cheap.

Analysts had at one point described Marsh as 'catatonic' but the merger now gives it a very strong world position. J&H, which had revenues of $1.2 billion in 1996, is highly regarded in the U.S. and has excellent links with brokers in other partners of the world through its UNISON strategic alliance. The deal follows the $200m acquisition by Marsh of French broker CECAR last month which, combined with its existing French operation, gave it a lead role in that market. Marsh is also in talks to buy London market Minet which have been dragging on for several months.
But for the other players in the broking sector, and for international insurers and reinsurers, the emergence of two superbrokers in the space of a few months has other ramifications.

Most under pressure are Sedgwick and Willis, whose positions are completely overshadowed. Sedgwick has said it would like to merge with a suitable partner but has not yet found one, while the slightly smaller Willis has said it would prefer to grow organically.

Both have refuted suggestions that they should merge with each other and, because in many ways they replicate each other, neither has been sure what a merger would really add. But as a result of today's merger, they will come under renewed pressure to get together and form a sizeable British counterweight to domination by Marsh and Aon.

A merger could be costly in terms of job losses because of the high level of duplication, but it might allow the formation of a high quality international broker with a dominant influence in Lloyd's and the London market.

The realities they face have also changed. Broker consolidation has been driven not only by declining commissions but by the need to be able to serve global clients wherever they are in the world. The existence of two superbrokers will raise the threshold of the critical mass required to offer top quality global service.
At the same time the giants may be able to push their cost base down to a level which makes it more difficult for smaller companies to compete.

And as insurance broking depends largely on individuals producing business through personal relationships with clients, there is the danger that Marsh and Aon will have the clout to tempt the best people away from rival firms.

For insurers and reinsurers the issues are slightly different. Some believe that the reduction in the number of competing brokers will ease the downward pressure on insurance rates. Others say the new super-brokers will have powerful bargaining positions, and will exert a strong influence on rates in their clients' favour.

There is likely to be a continued flight to quality in which the top brokers insist on dealing only with insurers with top-notch security ratings. This could trigger more consolidation among insurers and reinsurers, and accelerate the flow of corporate capital into Lloyd's of London.

The creation of J&H Marsh & McLennan is unlikely to be the last move in the consolidation of the industry, but if it creates the second of the two giants which dominate insurance for the foreseeable future, it will be the most significant. No text received
